title: Russia Suspended From World Chess. India’s Gukesh and Vaishali Are Waiting on the Other Side.
excerpt: FIDE has banned Russia’s chess federation after it refused to stop holding events in occupied Ukraine. Meanwhile, India now has two players — a brother-sister pair among them — preparing to challenge for world titles.
body:
For decades, Russia was chess. From Spassky to Karpov to Kasparov, the country dominated the game with a grip so tight it seemed genetic. On Wednesday, the International Chess Federation suspended Russia’s membership with immediate effect.

The suspension — triggered by Russia’s refusal to stop organising chess events in occupied Ukrainian territories — marks the end of an era that was already dying. Only one Russian player currently sits in the world’s top 20. The country’s last world champion, Garry Kasparov, retired from competitive play in 2005. The players who now define chess come from elsewhere.

They come, increasingly, from India.

## The Crown and the Challenger

Gukesh Dommaraju, 20 years old and from Chennai, is the reigning World Chess Champion — the youngest undisputed champion in the history of the game. He won the title in Singapore in December 2024, defeating China’s Ding Liren in a match that was tied heading into the final game. Later this year, between November 23 and December 17, he will defend it against Javokhir Sindarov of Uzbekistan, the 20-year-old who won the 2026 Candidates Tournament.

It will be a collision of prodigies. Both players will be under 21 during the match. Both have broken records that once belonged to Kasparov’s generation. And both represent a chess world that has moved decisively away from Russia’s orbit.

But Gukesh is not the only Indian preparing for a world title match. His compatriot Vaishali Rameshbabu — R Praggnanandhaa’s elder sister — won the Women’s Candidates Tournament in April, finishing with 8.5 out of 14 points in Cyprus. She will challenge China’s Ju Wenjun for the Women’s World Championship, the dates and venue still to be announced.

Vaishali entered the tournament as the lowest-rated player in the field. She left it as the clear winner, having defeated higher-rated opponents with a blend of deep preparation and composure under pressure. Her brother, Praggnanandhaa, who also competed in the open Candidates, travelled with the family to Cyprus and served as part of her support team.

## What the Suspension Means

The FIDE suspension stems from a Court of Arbitration for Sport ruling in March. CAS found that Russia’s chess federation had incorporated chess organisations in Crimea, Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson, and Zaporizhzhia — territories internationally recognised as Ukrainian — and gave Russia 90 days to withdraw. Russia did not comply.

Under the suspension, Russia cannot vote in FIDE assemblies, nominate officers, or participate in team competitions. Individual Russian players can still compete in FIDE events, but only under FIDE’s flag — not Russia’s. The suspension can last up to three years or until compliance is achieved.

Critics have noted that FIDE, whose president Arkady Dvorkovich is a former Russian deputy prime minister, left a potential loophole: Russian teams “may be eligible” for team events under a neutral flag, subject to further decisions. That could theoretically allow Russian participation in the Chess Olympiad in Uzbekistan this September. The English Chess Federation’s Dominic Lawson called the situation “humiliating for Russia” but pushed for stricter enforcement.

## Why This Matters for the Diaspora

India’s rise in chess is a source of quiet, sustained pride for the diaspora. Viswanathan Anand — who held the world title from 2007 to 2013 — remains the spiritual godfather of Indian chess, and at 56, he is still competing in the inaugural Total Chess World Championship, qualified through rating. Arjun Erigaisi, ranked eighth in the world, R Praggnanandhaa, ranked 16th, and Wesley So, the Filipino-American grandmaster ranked ninth, all feature in that event as well.

For NRI families across the United States, the United Kingdom, and Canada, chess has long been a cultural bridge — a pursuit that carries the same weight as academic achievement and classical music. The sight of Gukesh lifting the world championship trophy in Singapore resonated in living rooms from Edison to Hounslow to Brampton.

Now, with Russia sidelined and India fielding two world championship challengers from the same family, the symbolism is hard to miss. The old power has been suspended. The new one is not waiting for permission.
